metadata.prompt: A tree-diagram of a website's structure where generic branch names lead to a single sinister red leaf.
A small, pixelated figure holding a large cardboard cutout of a trusted CEO's face.
A URL bar with microsoft.update.secure-portal.net where 'microsoft' is in bright blue and 'secure-portal.net' is in grey.
A diagram showing a URL sequence where the text to the right of the last dot is highlighted as the 'Owner'.
A smartphone on a desk showing an incoming text message from 'POLICE' with a suspicious link inside.
A white theater mask being pulled away by a wire, revealing a red digital error code underneath.
A digital magnifying glass focusing on the very end of a URL string: ...legit-site.com.ATTACK.xyz.

content.narrative: The attacker is evolving. You’ve learned to spot the fake sender. You’ve learned to hover. But what happens when the link starts with a name you trust? This is Subdomain Manipulation. An attacker might create a link like 'microsoft.security-update.com'. At a glance, your brain sees 'Microsoft'. But in the architecture of the web, the True Domain is always the part immediately before the final extension. And then there is the Masked Display Name. Attackers will set their phone number or email name to 'INTERNAL ALERT'. When the notification hits your screen, you don't see the source address, just the alarming label. It is a clever wrapper. The protocol remains unchanged: Peel back the label. Always look for the Root Domain. Signal analysis must be absolute.
content.speaker: Rogue AI

content: Definition: Using trusted names as labels for fake domains
Rule: The Root Domain is the true owner
Tactic: Masked Display Names on Mobile/SMS

content.question: In the URL microsoft.support-portal.net/auth, who is the actual owner of the website?
